newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: France's influence seen under threat in Caribbean.
newsitem.headline: France's influence seen under threat in Caribbean.

text.p: As U.S. President Bill Clinton presses Caribbean leaders to boost free trade in the region at a summit in Barbados on Saturday, France's influence in the region seems under threat, officials said.
In Africa, the looming defeat of Zaire's long-time French-backed strongman, President Mobutu Sese Seko, has highlighted France's loss of sway to the United States.
In the Caribbean, the latest episode in the transatlantic "banana war" has dealt a potential blow to French influence, which had remained strong, if historically more discreet.

A successful U.S. challenge in the World Trade Organisation to a European Union banana import system that favours former European colonies, mainly in the Caribbean islands, over South and Central American producers, has given Washington the upper hand in negotiations.

Bananas account for 90 percent of export earnings in St. Lucia, 65 percent in St. Vincent and Dominica and a substantial portion of the earnings of Jamaica, Grenada and Surinam -- countries that have until now benefited from the EU regime.

A WTO panel found this month that the EU discriminates against bananas marketed by U.S. firms, which operate mainly in Central America. The EU is expected to appeal and a final WTO ruling may not come till the end of this year.
Caribbean nations may be uncomfortable with Washington's intentions in the region, but the EU no longer seems in a position to counterbalance U.S. influence, local leaders say.

Jamaica's Prime Minister P.J. Patterson who will chair the Barbados summit said: "We have made every effort to communicate the deleterious effects of the WTO ruling would have, even on non-producing states, should it bring the (EU) regime to an abrupt halt.
"We think (the summit will) have to find other means by which continuing access can be assured," for banana exports.

French President Jacques Chirac laid down a challenge to U.S. dominance in the Western hemisphere when he toured South America in March, urging the powerful Mercosur group -- Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay -- to build a privileged relationship with Europe.

The French Caribbean islands Martinique and Guadeloupe, and French Guiana on the north-east coast of South America, the only non-independent territory on the Western Hemisphere's mainland, are the only full-fledged EU territories in the region.
Yet despite efforts by successive French governments, Paris has failed to integrate its territories into the economy and institutions of the region.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, on a visit to the region a year ago, urged France's territories to take advantage of business tax breaks to boost local development.
But Paris' plans have been marred by increased economic and social problems in the territories.

French Guiana was rocked last month by a wave of rioting in its capital Cayenne, triggered by the arrest of 11 people including four leading members of the territory's independence movement, for allegedly setting fire to the home of French Guiana's state prosecutor during previous riots in November.

All were transferred to Martinique and Guadeloupe, where their presence has aggravated those islands' tense economic and social balance. Strikes in support of the independence leaders closed down municipal services in several towns.
The riots in French Guiana have undermined the French overseas department's tranquil facade and laid bare economic, political and social woes.
Citizens of the French Caribbean territories have full French, and hence European Union citizenship.
But the territories lag behind mainland France in housing, education and health. Unemployment exceeds 20 percent and their economies are heavily dependent on subsidies from Paris and Brussels.
Of greatest strategic interest is the European Space Agency's Ariane rocket launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana.
Though space activity accounts for well over half the economy of French Guiana, few in France's equatorial backwater see the centre as a motor for increased economic development.
